title: AGNTCon + MCPCon 2026: Agentic AI Foundation Adds Four Projects as MCP Turns to Security
summary:
At AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026, the Agentic AI Foundation added OpenSandbox, Open Responses, Agent Skills, and OpenEnv, reaching ten projects in its first year. Keynotes from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and UC Berkeley focused on MCP in production, security, and agents with their own identities.

By Andrew Hoblitzell

title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
summary:
Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox

webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error.

It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine.

It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright.

I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used:

Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory)

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the re

  • Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set

title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
summary: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.

title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
story_key: story|title:turning database grading into rl rewards post training agents with thinkingbox
content_excerpt: This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub . We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps. Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post , we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row. Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function. + So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing. Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it. We call this offline policy-relative difficulty . We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run. We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt. Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool. Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loo

title: Building live intelligence: Databricks AI Search supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg
summary: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed...
story_key: story|title:building live intelligence databricks ai search supports streaming tables materi
content_excerpt: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg v3+ in addition to Delta tables. You can bring live events, continuously maintained personalized state, and open-format data directly into your AI Search applications — reducing the overhead of building and managing separate pipelines to convert and synchronize these data sources. Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed Iceberg each represent a different way of working with data, and each opens up new possibilities for AI applications. Continuously changing data such as new listings, inventory, availability, and user activity can flow into an append-only Streaming Table, with AI Search indexing new records as they arrive and keeping the search index up to date. This freshness enables applications where the latest data can directly shape the search experience: helping users discover newly available restaurants through a search bar, or generating real-time recommendations based on recent trends. Materialized Views can aggregate events, filter records, and join data from multiple sources to create customized state. As the underlying data changes, the view is incrementally maintained and AI Search propagates those changes to the index, enabling personalized search experiences such as session-aware recommendations, product and content discovery based on recent activity, or tailor results to a user's evolving interests and preferences. Managed Iceberg tables can serve as AI Search sources directly, without conversion or migration to another table format, making open-format data available to search indexes and other AI applications. The open-format enables AI applications that work across existing data environments: search across product catalogs managed by different systems, unify business or customer data stored across Managed Iceberg tables, or build search experiences over large, distributed datasets without moving the underlying data. Before native support, customers had to create a separate Delta representation of Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables and build pipelines to keep it synchronized with the source. This added an extra data layer, custom update logic, and ongoing operational overhead. Now, AI Search connects directly to these sources. title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work.
story_key: story|title:the five components of building a company harness
content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference
summary: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.

title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.

title: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference
summary: Introducing Humming, a quantized inference kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community, with broad GPU and quantization support, dense and MoE performance results, and vLLM integration.
story_key: story|variant:quantized|title:announcing humming fast flexible kernels for quantized inference
content_excerpt: Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features: As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency. Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space. These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low. Developing and integrating a dedicated kernel for every combination creates a growing maintenance burden. Each addition can require its own weight preprocessing, kernel selection, framework adapters, and tests. Optimizations must then be carried across multiple implementations. Humming addresses this problem by separating quantization descriptions from execution choices and composing kernels from shared components. Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components. Models exported by different quantization tools vary in numeric format, parameter organization, and weight layout. Humming converts supported export formats into the Humming standard format: a common quantization description with consistently organized weights, scales, zero points, and other tensors. title: Serverless routing made sticky
summary: Voice agents, multiplayer games, and other workloads can now build on Sticky Sessions. Achieve strong affinity without losing autoscaling. Here’s how we built this on Modal Servers.
story_key: story|title:serverless routing made sticky
content_excerpt: At Modal, our serverless compute powers real-time inference, training, and batch jobs, scaling automatically with demand. Sandboxes offer a different model, containers whose lifecycles you explicitly control. A growing number of workloads require something in-between; autoscaling serverless compute that maintains continuity between requests. Consider a speech-to-text model with decoder state for an audio stream, a voice agent that holds a conversation, or a multiplayer game . For these workloads, users must come back to the same container on every reconnect for the entirety of their session. We recently launched Sticky Sessions , built on top of our low-latency Modal Servers . Every session’s requests land on the same container. To use Sticky Sessions, just create a Modal Server with the @modal.sessioned() decorator and start the sessions with the SDK or the HTTP API : Modal has supported WebSockets via Web Functions for some time. However, a WebSocket connection is tied to a Function “input”, not a container—if the connection drops, a new input is created on reconnect and can land on a different container. Stateful web UIs such as Gradio and Streamlit are workloads that need strong affinity guarantees between requests and backend containers. Every request has to reach the process that holds the user’s state. One anti-pattern workaround is setting max_containers=1 , which guarantees stickiness by giving up scaling entirely. Modal Servers already provide a softer form of affinity ; requests that share the same Modal-Affinity-Routing-Key header are routed to the same container in a best-effort manner. The container can still be scaled down or replaced at any time, routing future requests to a different container. Sticky Sessions provide stronger routing guarantees by ensuring all requests in the same session land on the same container. Sticky Sessions build on the infrastructure we developed for Modal Servers . At the core of this infrastructure is our in-house stateless proxy (fprs). The proxy provides low-latency routing and load balancing using in-memory cached routing state reconciled from durable storage. Servers already give us a way to route HTTP traffic to a container, manage container lifecycles, and scale the fleet based on demand.
